anchor: Ring out wild bells to the wild sky
title: In Memoriam CVI: 'Ring out, wild bells'
short: Section CVI in standard numbering (titled CIV in this archive): New Year's Eve bells, turning the poet from private grief to hopes for humanity.
body: In Memoriam A. H. H. (published anonymously in 1850) mourns Arthur Henry Hallam, Tennyson's closest Cambridge friend and his sister Emily's fiancé, who died suddenly in Vienna on 15 September 1833. Its 131 sections and frame poems were written over some seventeen years. This is section CVI in the standard numbering, set on New Year's Eve after the move from Somersby. Bradley notes that the mood of CV continues and rises: the bells sound wild and jubilant, and the poet turns from grief to the future of man, favouring the powers that unite people. A local tradition connects the bells with Waltham Abbey near High Beech, where the Tennysons lived from 1837, but this is unproved. The section became a popular New Year text and hymn.

anchor: Ring out the old, ring in the new
title: Ring out ... ring in
short: Each stanza is built on paired commands, 'Ring out' the bad and 'ring in' the good, like the alternating peals of change-ringing.
body: The section's structure is a sequence of antitheses: out the old, in the new; out the false, in the true. The repeated imperatives imitate the bells' insistent rhythm and give the section the form of a public hymn or litany rather than the private brooding of most of In Memoriam. The In Memoriam stanza, with its enclosed abba rhyme, suits the call-and-response of 'out' and 'in'.

anchor: The year is dying in the night
title: The year is dying in the night
short: The old year as a dying man: 'let him die' gives permission to let go, a turning-point in the poet's grief.
body: Personifying the year as 'him' who dies in the night echoes the poem's real death, and 'let him die' / 'let him go' (l. 7) suggests release from mourning. Bradley notes that the poet turns from 'the grief that saps the mind' (l. 9), here rung out, to hope for others. The wild sky and frosty light set the scene in winter.

anchor: the grief that saps the mind
title: the grief that saps the mind
short: Private sorrow is now named as something that weakens the mind and must be let go.
body: To sap is to undermine, as by digging beneath a wall, or to drain of vital juices. Bradley comments that the feeling that his grief isolates him and is useless to others stirs the poet to overcome it. The personal is quickly joined to the social: the next line rings out 'the feud of rich and poor'. The phrase thus marks a turning point in the elegy as a whole, from private lament toward public hope.

anchor: the feud of rich and poor
title: the feud of rich and poor
short: Class conflict in the hungry 1840s, the time of Chartism and of Disraeli's 'two nations'.
body: The years in which much of In Memoriam was written were marked by economic distress and the Chartist movement for political reform (1838-48). Disraeli's novel Sybil (1845) described rich and poor as two nations. 'Redress to all mankind' hopes for remedy. Bradley cross-refers to the Prologue, l. 12, and observes that the forces the poet invokes are those that unite people.

title: a slowly dying cause, / And ancient forms of party strife
short: Outworn political causes and partisan conflicts, left unspecified.
body: The section avoids naming particular causes, and editors do not identify 'a slowly dying cause'; the vagueness lets the hope apply generally. The contrast 'nobler modes of life, / With sweeter manners, purer laws' sets moral and social reform against party politics. 'Manners' has its older sense of customs and morals. The hope is reformist rather than revolutionary: it asks for gentler manners and better laws, not the overthrow of institutions.

title: Ring out, ring out my mournful rhymes, / But ring the fuller minstrel in
short: The poet bids farewell to his own elegies and welcomes a greater poetry or poet to come.
body: The poem refers to itself: the 'mournful rhymes' are the sections of In Memoriam. The 'fuller minstrel' may be a future poet of fuller powers, or the poet's own voice in a fuller, more hopeful mode; the phrase does not decide. Bradley cross-refers these lines to the Prologue and to the Epilogue, the marriage song that ends the poem. 'The faithless coldness of the times' names a spiritual malaise of the age.

anchor: false pride in place and blood
title: false pride in place and blood
short: Snobbery of rank and birth: 'place' is social position, 'blood' aristocratic descent.
body: 'Place' means rank or office; 'blood' lineage. The line rejects aristocratic pride, a theme Tennyson treated in 'Lady Clara Vere de Vere' ('Kind hearts are more than coronets'). 'The civic slander and the spite' extends the criticism to the quarrels of town and public life. The section's social hopes are, typically for Tennyson, moral rather than programmatic: they ask for changed hearts more than for particular measures, and pair the vices of the privileged with the spite of public life.

title: old shapes of foul disease
short: Epidemics such as the cholera outbreaks of 1832 and 1848-49, and the filth of crowded towns.
body: Britain suffered cholera epidemics in 1831-32 and 1848-49, and the sanitary reform movement (Chadwick's report of 1842) was arguing that disease came from bad drainage and overcrowding. The hope to 'ring out old shapes of foul disease' is thus a concrete reform agenda as well as a millennial vision. Tennyson's list thus moves from social conflict and personal grief to the material conditions of life, and then to war and peace.

title: the narrowing lust of gold
short: Greed that narrows the soul; the love of money as 'the root of all evil'.
body: The line recalls 1 Timothy 6:10, 'the love of money is the root of all evil'. 'Narrowing' makes greed a contraction of sympathy, the opposite of 'The larger heart, the kindlier hand' in the next stanza. In the 1840s the railway speculation mania made money-lust a topical subject. The stanza joins disease, greed and war as evils of the old order, each paired with the hope that will replace it in the final stanza.

title: the thousand years of peace
short: The millennium: the thousand-year reign of peace prophesied in Revelation 20.
body: Revelation 20:1-6 foresees Satan bound for a thousand years while the saints reign with Christ; Isaiah 2:4 foresees nations beating swords into ploughshares. The 'thousand wars of old' are rung out and a thousand years of peace rung in, the numbers balanced. Victorian progressive thought often gave the millennium a secular form, a gradual improvement of society. The line prepares the section's final, explicitly Christian hope.

title: the darkness of the land
short: Spiritual and social darkness, set against the coming light of Christ.
body: Bradley compares the antithesis with section XXX, where the Christmas Eve singers turn from darkness to the hope of light. The phrase may also recall the darkness 'over all the land' at the crucifixion (Matthew 27:45) and Isaiah's people who walked in darkness and saw a great light (Isaiah 9:2), so that the final line brings dawn after the long night.

anchor: the Christ that is to be
title: Ring in the Christ that is to be
short: A future Christ: the second coming, or the spirit of Christ realised in human society. Tennyson explained it as Christianity without bigotry.
body: The Memoir (I.325-326), quoted by Bradley, reports Tennyson's conviction that the forms of the Christian religion would alter but the spirit of Christ would grow 'from more to more'; one of his meanings for this line was a time when Christianity without bigotry would triumph and controversies of creed would vanish. Some readers take the line as orthodox expectation of the Second Coming; others as a liberal, even evolutionary idea of a Christ realised progressively in mankind. Tennyson's 'one of my meanings' allows both.
